_readme: SUNNYVAiLE High — the video classes. Each TOOL is a SUBJECT; each subject has eight short single-topic PERIODS. One classroom, one chalkboard, one AV cart; only the chalk and the tape change. A class is a row here, never a new page. Wrapper: /learn/class.html?c=<slug>
_structure: Ali 2026-07-22: tool-first, not concept-first. Eight short classes per tool beats one long deep dive, because vendor feature names rot fast — a rename then costs ONE re-shoot instead of the whole lesson. Same eight periods in the same order for every subject, so one script is filmed three times.
_order: ChatGPT ships complete first, then Claude, then Gemini. Gemini last deliberately — the research flagged it as the most volatile of the five.
_research: operations/research/tool-machinery/ — every path and mistake below traces to a vendor page with a checked date.

subjects.name: The Basics
subjects.note: Cross-tool. Teaches each concept ONCE so the tool subjects only have to show where it lives. No vendor feature names appear in it, so nothing in it goes stale.

subjects.name: Reality Check Lab
subjects.note: Cross-tool intermediate labs for testing popular AI claims against the complete operating workflow.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: What You're Looking At
classes.subtitle: The app around the model, the context it supplies, and where verification still belongs
classes.question: I have it open. What am I actually looking at?
learn: Distinguish the app or assistant from the model
Trace how instructions, files, search and tool results can become working context
Choose one real task and name what still needs verification
path: Start with one ordinary task. Name the product or app handling the request.
Name the model as one component inside that product—not the whole experience.
Mark what the app deliberately supplies as working context: your request, instructions, conversation, files, memory or selected tool results.
Name any optional capability the app uses, such as search, file handling, calculation or a connected service.
Finish with the human boundary: the claim, decision or outcome that still needs checking.
classes.mistake: Treating a polished answer as proof that you know where it came from. Fluency does not tell you whether the response was generated from patterns, grounded in a current source, shaped by saved context or checked against the real world.
classes.analogy: Think of the app as a studio, the model as one performer and tools as equipment the studio may make available. It helps separate the cast; it is not a technical blueprint, and the model is not a person.
classes.mechanism: The app assembles the instructions and working context for the task. A model processes what it is given and produces—or helps select—the next output or action. If the app uses search, files or another tool, selected results can be added to that context. None of those layers makes an important claim automatically true.

demo.variable: whether a current source is supplied as working context
demo.task: A colleague asks whether a newly announced reimbursement rule applies to an expense submitted on Friday.

bad.input: Does the new reimbursement rule apply to an expense I submit on Friday?
bad.output: Yes. New reimbursement rules generally apply to all expenses submitted after they are announced.
bad.verdict: It sounds decisive, but no rule, date or responsible source was supplied. The answer filled the gap with a plausible generalisation.

demo.why: The model only had the question. It did not have the operative rule or a current source, so there was no evidence for the confident conclusion.
demo.fix: Give the app the responsible source—or use a visible search capability to find it—then require the answer to identify the exact sentence and effective date it relies on.

good.input: Using only the attached policy notice, tell me whether the rule applies to an expense submitted on Friday. Quote the effective-date sentence. If the notice does not settle it, say what is missing.
good.output: The notice says the rule applies to expenses submitted on or after Monday. A Friday submission falls before that date. I would still confirm that no later notice replaced this one.
good.verdict: The source entered the working context, the conclusion points to its evidence and the remaining verification boundary stays visible.

practice.title: Map one task before you hand it over
practice.intro: Choose a real, low-risk task. The map makes you name what each layer is doing—and what remains yours to judge.
practice.explain_back_prompt: In your own words: why is an AI app more than a model?

take_home.title: The App / Model / Context / Check map
take_home.description: Keep the map beside any AI task: what you want, what the app must supply, what capability may help, what must be verified and what private information stays out.

book.name: The Glossary
book.why: Look up model, context, retrieval, memory and the other words products often blur together.

episode.name: Episode 01 · On Wednesdays We Do AI
episode.why: Return to the story that opens the first safe interaction with AI.

classes.subject: reality-check
classes.name: What the Viral Reel Left Out
classes.chalk: What the Viral Reel Left Out
classes.subtitle: How to turn a shiny AI claim into a workflow that can survive real life
classes.question: It looked effortless in the reel. What did the jump cut leave out?
learn: Classify an AI claim without blaming yourself when the demo skipped the setup
Find the prerequisites, configuration, judgement, boundaries, tests and upkeep hidden by the jump cut
Run one bounded test and choose build, revise, investigate, decline or monitor
path: Write down the exact promised outcome without the promotional adjectives.
Confirm the current capability from the responsible product source.
Fill in the missing prerequisites, setup, human judgement and stop conditions.
Test a normal case, an edge case and a case that should stop.
Decide what happens next from the evidence—not from how smooth the demo looked.
classes.mistake: Treating one polished demonstration as a complete workflow—and treating the gap between the demonstration and real life as personal failure.
classes.analogy: A viral AI reel is a makeover montage: it can show the reveal while skipping the fittings, lighting, tailoring and person checking the mirror. The analogy explains the jump cut; it does not mean AI work is cosmetic or effortless.
classes.mechanism: A feature is one capability. A dependable workflow also needs an intended outcome, authorized inputs, configuration, human-owned decisions, boundaries, tests and upkeep. Product access and behavior can change, so the responsible source and the working setup both need dates.

demo.variable: whether the operating setup and acceptance evidence are defined before relying on the result
demo.task: Assess the claim that installing a reusable AI skill lets it handle a department's work.

bad.input: Install the skill, try one favorable example and use the polished result as proof that the department workflow is ready.
bad.output: The first output looks convincing, so the workflow is treated as complete.
bad.verdict: The capability may be real, but the conclusion skipped permissions, trusted inputs, failure behavior, human accountability and maintenance.

demo.why: A reusable skill can package instructions, examples, resources and code. That does not make it accountable staff or prove it has the access, evidence and controls required for a real department workflow.
demo.fix: Define the bounded job, authorized material, permissions, human checkpoint, stop conditions and acceptance tests before deciding whether to build.

good.input: Using fictional material only, test the skill on one normal case, one edge case and one stop case. Record the expected result, the human decision and the evidence required before use.
good.output: The capability is separated from the operating setup, failures stay visible and the next decision is based on declared evidence.
good.verdict: The workflow can now be built, revised, investigated, declined or monitored without pretending one good output proved the whole promise.

practice.title: Build the part the reel skipped
practice.intro: Use the guided claim, a low-risk practice, or a current claim of your own. The card turns the jump cut into a workflow you can test without handing over your judgement.
practice.check_title: Can you spot the jump cut?

guided.claim: Install a reusable AI skill and it can handle a department's work.
guided.outcome: A repeatable, bounded task is completed consistently enough for a named person to review and use.
guided.capability: A reusable skill can package instructions, examples, resources and code. Availability, permissions and behavior depend on the current product, plan and workspace configuration.
guided.prerequisites: An eligible account; an approved skill; a bounded task; authorized source material; the minimum necessary access; a named owner.
guided.setup: Define inputs, instructions, examples, allowed tools, output format, escalation path and the evidence the reviewer must see.
guided.judgement: A named person decides whether the result is accurate, appropriate and ready to use. The skill does not own the consequence.
guided.boundaries: No private or consequential material in the trial. Stop on missing evidence, unexpected access, conflicting instructions or an output outside the bounded task.
guided.normal: Run a fictional routine example with a known expected answer.
guided.edge: Run an incomplete or ambiguous example and confirm the workflow asks for what is missing.
guided.stop: Offer prohibited or unsupported material and confirm the workflow refuses or escalates.
guided.acceptance: All three cases follow the declared boundary; evidence is visible; the human reviewer can explain why the result passed or failed.
guided.upkeep: The workflow owner re-checks after a product, permission, instruction, source or job change and can roll back to the last known version.
guided.reason: The reusable capability is real, but the department-work promise needs a bounded job, controls and evidence before it can be built responsibly.
guided.status: Guided practice loaded. It uses fictional material and a current product claim checked on August 2, 2026.

low-risk.claim: Give AI the meeting notes and it will handle every follow-up.
low-risk.outcome: Turn fictional meeting notes into a draft list of owners, actions and due dates for a person to confirm.
low-risk.capability: A model can extract and structure information that appears in supplied notes; it cannot recover decisions or dates that were never recorded.
low-risk.prerequisites: Fictional notes, a declared output format and a reviewer who attended the meeting or owns the record.
low-risk.setup: Ask for quoted evidence beside every proposed action and require missing owners or dates to be marked as missing.
low-risk.judgement: The meeting owner confirms that each action, owner and date reflects what was actually agreed.
low-risk.boundaries: Do not paste confidential notes into an unapproved product. Stop rather than invent an owner, decision or deadline.
low-risk.normal: Notes clearly state an action, owner and date.
low-risk.edge: The action is clear but the owner or date is missing.
low-risk.stop: The notes contain a sensitive personnel issue that should not enter this tool.
low-risk.acceptance: Every extracted item points to evidence; missing details stay missing; the stop case is excluded.
low-risk.upkeep: Re-check the prompt if the meeting template, approved tool or information policy changes.
low-risk.reason: The low-risk draft saves time while the responsible person still verifies the record and owns every follow-up.
low-risk.status: Low-risk practice loaded. The scenario is fictional and keeps private meeting material out.

advanced.status: Advanced practice loaded. Start with a current primary source and a claim you genuinely want to use.

take_home.description: Take the completed card with you as accessible HTML. It records the promise, operating setup, human decision, tests, boundaries and upkeep in one place.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: Why It Doesn't Know About Last Month
classes.chalk: Why It Doesn't Know About Last Month
classes.subtitle: Versions, cutoffs, and how it looks things up
classes.question: Why is it confidently telling me something that stopped being true?
learn: Understand what a training cutoff is
Spot a stale answer
Know that searching is how it gets current
classes.analogy: Textbook editions — once printed the words can't change; the cutoff is the print date; web search is the teacher's photocopied handout.
classes.note: LOCKED canon analogy. Was flagged MISSING by Codex — now in the list.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: What It Can See Right Now
classes.chalk: What It Can See Right Now
classes.subtitle: Context — the finite space it works from in this conversation
classes.question: It was good this morning. Why is it worse now?
learn: See what counts as 'in front of it' right now
Know why a long chat degrades
Learn to put what matters where it can be read
classes.analogy: The chalkboard — a finite space; when it fills, older material has to be erased or condensed to make room.
classes.mechanism: The model works only from what is supplied in the current conversation. If something is not in it, it fills the gap with the most likely average.

demo.variable: whether the brief is present in the current conversation — two fresh chats, nothing else different
demo.task: The identical request, made in two fresh chats: one with no brief in it, one where an earlier line holds the brief.

bad.input: [fresh chat, no brief]  Give me three headline options.
bad.output:
Introducing Our Exciting New Update — Everything You Need to Know Today!

Big News: Something Special Has Finally Arrived!

You Won't Want to Miss What's New!
bad.verdict: Long, exclamation marks, could be about anything.

demo.why: The model works only from what is in this conversation, and the brief is not in it. So it fills the gap with the average.
demo.fix: Put the brief in the conversation first.

good.input:
[fresh chat]  Headlines: under eight words, no exclamation marks, for a business software update.
Give me three headline options.
good.output:
The New Update Is Here

Six Months of Work, Shipped

Everything We Rebuilt This Quarter
good.verdict: Identical request. The only difference was whether the brief was in the current conversation.

classes.note: Codex fix: chalkboard keeps 'finite space' but drops 'wiped at the top' (products may omit/summarise/select, not strict first-out).

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: What's Saved vs What's In the Room
classes.chalk: What's Saved vs What's In the Room
classes.subtitle: History, context and memory are three different things
classes.question: It remembered that yesterday — why not now?
learn: Tell a saved old chat from the current conversation
Know that opening an old chat is not the same as it being 'in the room'
See where each of the three lives
classes.note: Codex: beginners conflate history / context / memory. Explicit short class to separate them, sits between context and memory.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: What It Has Stored About You
classes.chalk: What It Has Stored About You
classes.subtitle: Memory — a note the tool writes and keeps
classes.question: What has it quietly written down about me?
learn: Find what the tool has stored
Correct one entry, delete another
See why deleting a chat doesn't delete the note
classes.analogy: The Blend & Snap — a new café can't give you the usual; your regular can, because you built it over a hundred Tuesdays. Stated after the plain mechanics, never as the mechanics.
classes.mechanism: The tool stores a note about you and hands it to the model. The model has not humanly learned you — it is given the note each time.

demo.variable: whether the saved note is supplied to the model — same account, same prompt, same facts, only the memory toggle flips
demo.task: The identical request, which itself contains the facts, run twice — once with saved memory off, once on.

bad.input: Write a note to my team: the supplier missed Friday, so the report lands Wednesday.  [saved memory OFF]
bad.output: Dear Team, I wanted to take a moment to reach out regarding the delay with our supplier. The report will now be ready on Wednesday. Apologies for any inconvenience...
bad.verdict: Wordy, apologetic, generic — the average business-email voice.

demo.why: With nothing about how you write to narrow it, the most likely output is the average version. Your style was not supplied, so it produced the middle of the road.
demo.fix: Not a longer prompt. The saved note — that you write short and do not apologise twice — turned on.

good.input: Write a note to my team: the supplier missed Friday, so the report lands Wednesday.  [saved memory ON]
good.output: Team — supplier missed Friday, report lands Wednesday. Nothing else moves.
good.verdict: Same account, same words, same facts. The only change was whether the tool handed the model your saved note. The good output invents nothing — the facts came from the prompt, the style from the note.

classes.note: Boundary per Codex: the tool stores/supplies; the model does not 'learn' you.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: What to Set Up Once
classes.subtitle: Custom instructions — a standing note you write yourself
classes.question: How do I stop re-explaining myself every time?
learn: Write a standing note that applies to new chats
Know what belongs here vs in memory
Know it can be scoped or overridden, not absolute
classes.analogy: A standing-order card the customer writes herself — as opposed to memory, which is the note the tool writes about you.
classes.note: Codex key fix: memory vs custom instructions split on AUTHORSHIP. ⚠ not 'applies to everything after' — applied to new chats going forward; a tool can scope/override.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: What's Saved and What You're Granting
classes.chalk: What's Saved and What You're Granting
classes.subtitle: Permissions and data controls — the prerequisite
classes.question: What is actually being kept, and what did I just allow?
learn: See what a tool saves by default
Know what you granted, and how to take it back
Do this before connecting anything
classes.note: Codex: essential prerequisite before files/memory/connectors. Was missing.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: Giving It Your Stuff
classes.subtitle: Files — and that the model may get a processed version, not your original
classes.question: If I upload this, what does it actually get?
learn: Hand it a file to work from
Know the model may get extracted text, not the original
Check that what you meant actually reached it
classes.analogy: A tailor working from fabric you bring — but the 'what actually reaches the model' point is shown plainly, not forced into the metaphor.
classes.note: Codex: the processed-representation point is the real lesson.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: Plugging It Into Your Life, Safely
classes.chalk: Plugging It Into Your Life, Safely
classes.subtitle: Connectors — scoped access to a service you already have
classes.question: If I connect my email, what can it really see?
learn: Connect one service and read the consent screen
Understand it's scoped access, not all-or-nothing
Actually revoke it
classes.analogy: A visitor pass to one filing cabinet, with the permissions printed on it — not an address book, which would imply handing over everything.
classes.note: Codex fix: address book implied wrong data shape + all-or-nothing.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: A Place for One Job
classes.subtitle: Projects — a persistent home for a job's files and instructions
classes.question: I keep re-explaining the same job. Where does it live?
learn: Make a place that holds a job's files and standing directions
Know it persists across chats
Know its items are available, not force-fed into every answer
classes.analogy: A Trapper Keeper subject section — the papers and the standing directions for one subject, kept together and kept over time.
classes.note: Codex fix: fitting room was temporary/cleared — wrong for a persistent workspace.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: Teaching It a Repeatable Job
classes.subtitle: Skills — a saved procedure done the same way each time
classes.question: Can I stop re-explaining how I like this done?
learn: Save a procedure so a job runs the same way
Know it repeats the steps, not an identical result
Know when to reach for one
classes.analogy: A recipe card — consistent steps, not an identical dish; generated results still vary.
classes.note: Codex fix: 'same result' was wrong. Automatic selection is product-specific → tool subject.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: Bolting On Extra Powers
classes.subtitle: Extensions and plug-ins — installed packages, and what runs where
classes.question: Everyone says to install this. Should I?
learn: Tell a plug-in from a skill from a connector
Ask what runs on your own computer before installing
Turn one off again
classes.analogy: A Trapper Keeper accessory pack — dividers, a calendar, a pouch, installed together — not a single recipe card.
classes.note: Codex: recipe card doesn't stretch to a bundle. Local-vs-remote code = a direct safety line.

classes.subject: basics
classes.name: Making It Run Without You
classes.subtitle: Scheduled tasks — the same job, on a schedule, unattended
classes.question: Can it just do this every Monday without me?
learn: Set a job that runs on a schedule
Find and manage the ones running
Know permissions and unattended runs vary by tool
classes.note: Hooks (event triggers) were CUT from Basics per Codex — advanced only.

classes.subject: chatgpt
classes.name: The Tour
classes.subtitle: Every part of the screen, named
classes.question: What is all of this, and which bits do I actually get?
path: Start on a blank chat and name the parts out loud, left to right
Sidebar — chats, Projects, GPTs, Plugins, Scheduled, Library
Composer — the + button, the tools menu, the voice icon
Model picker — what the names mean and why they change
Profile menu → Settings — where everything in this subject lives
classes.mistake: Assuming the screen you were handed is the only screen there is. Most of what ChatGPT does is behind the + button and the Settings menu, and nothing in the interface tells you to look there.
classes.tier: Free · Go · Plus · Pro — the tour covers what each tier actually shows
learn: Name every part of the screen
Find the settings that matter
Know what your plan actually includes
classes.blocked_reason: Menu paths came from vendor help centres, not the app. Proven unreliable 2026-07-22 (ChatGPT's shipped Settings has Hooks, Appshots, Pets, Computer use, Worktrees — none in the docs I read). Do not film until confirmed in the app.

classes.subject: chatgpt
classes.name: What It Already Knows About You
classes.subtitle: Memory — see it, edit it, delete it
classes.question: What has it quietly written down about me?
path: Settings → Personalization → Memory
Toggle Enable memory on, and read the memory summary aloud
Type into the box under the summary to correct it
Highlight one line in the summary to fix just that part
classes.mistake: Thinking that deleting the memory summary erases everything it knows about you. It does not — the chats, archived chats, files and connected-app content that carry the same facts are separate sources, and each has to be deleted on its own.
classes.tier: All tiers have memory; the amount is rationed by plan — Free limited, Pro maximum
learn: Open the memory screen
Edit and delete what is stored
See why deleting a chat is not enough
classes.blocked_reason: Menu paths came from vendor help centres, not the app. Proven unreliable 2026-07-22 (ChatGPT's shipped Settings has Hooks, Appshots, Pets, Computer use, Worktrees — none in the docs I read). Do not film until confirmed in the app.

classes.subject: chatgpt
classes.name: Set It Once
classes.subtitle: Custom instructions — stop retyping who you are
classes.question: How do I tell it how I work, once, and have it stick?
path: Settings → Personalization → turn Enable customization ON
Write into the Custom Instructions field
Open a brand-new chat and watch it obey with nothing pasted in
On phone the path differs: Settings → Customize ChatGPT
classes.mistake: Treating this box as private. OpenAI's own documentation warns that if you use third-party plug-ins, the model may pass relevant parts of your instructions to the plug-in developer.
classes.tier: Every plan — but the size is tiered: Free and Go 1,500 characters, Plus and Pro 5,000
learn: Write a standing instruction
Know what belongs there vs a single prompt
Understand who else can see it
classes.blocked_reason: Menu paths came from vendor help centres, not the app. Proven unreliable 2026-07-22 (ChatGPT's shipped Settings has Hooks, Appshots, Pets, Computer use, Worktrees — none in the docs I read). Do not film until confirmed in the app.

classes.subject: chatgpt
classes.name: A Room of Its Own
classes.subtitle: Projects — when a folder beats a conversation
classes.question: I keep re-explaining the same job. Where do I put it once?
path: Sidebar → New project → name it, pick a colour
Drop files into the project's upload area
Three-dot menu, top right → Project settings → project instructions
Drag an existing chat in via its menu → Move to project
classes.mistake: Assuming a project can always see your general ChatGPT memory. Whether it can depends on a choice made when the project was created — and sharing a project switches it to project-only memory permanently, which cannot be undone.
classes.tier: All plans, but file counts are tiered — Free 5 files, Go and Plus 25, Pro 40
learn: Make a project and add files
Set instructions that apply only there
Avoid the memory trap when you share one

classes.subject: chatgpt
classes.name: The Thing Beside the Chat
classes.subtitle: Canvas — editing a document instead of reading it back
classes.question: Something opened next to my chat. What is it and can I keep it?
path: Ask for something long, or type / and pick canvas
Highlight one paragraph and ask for a targeted fix
Use the built-in shortcuts — adjust length, change reading level
Step back through version history
classes.mistake: Assuming canvas always works. It is tied to specific model families — OpenAI states plainly that canvas is not supported on GPT-5.5 or later, so picking the newest model silently takes the feature away.
classes.tier: Every plan, on web and desktop. Not on mobile yet
learn: Open canvas on purpose
Edit one paragraph without redoing the rest
Understand why it sometimes refuses to open

classes.subject: chatgpt
classes.name: Same Question, Two Answers
classes.subtitle: The model picker, and why the choice changes the reply
classes.question: Does it matter which one of these I pick?
path: Ask one real question on a fast model. Keep the answer on screen
Ask the identical question on a slower reasoning model
Put the two answers side by side and read the difference out loud
Name the trade — speed against depth — and when each is worth it
classes.mistake: Believing the newest option is always the better one. It is a trade, not a ranking — and some features quietly switch off on newer models.
classes.tier: Which models appear depends on your plan
learn: Read the model picker
Ask the same thing two ways
Choose on purpose instead of by default
classes.blocked_reason: Menu paths came from vendor help centres, not the app. Proven unreliable 2026-07-22 (ChatGPT's shipped Settings has Hooks, Appshots, Pets, Computer use, Worktrees — none in the docs I read). Do not film until confirmed in the app.

classes.subject: chatgpt
classes.name: What You're Actually Granting
classes.subtitle: Apps and connectors — read the screen before you tap Allow
classes.question: If I connect my email, what can it really see?
path: Composer + → More, or the Plugins Directory in the sidebar
Pick one, hit Connect, and read the authorisation screen line by line
Settings → Apps → App Preferences → set when it asks permission
Settings → Apps → disconnect — this is the only real revoke
classes.mistake: Thinking the permission setting controls what an app can reach. It does not. OpenAI is explicit: permissions only change when ChatGPT asks before using access it already has. To actually take access away you have to disconnect the app.
classes.tier: Varies by plan, workspace, role and region — there is no published table
learn: Read an authorisation screen properly
Set when it asks permission
Actually revoke access

classes.subject: chatgpt
classes.name: While You're Asleep
classes.subtitle: Scheduled tasks — it works without you sitting there
classes.question: Can it just do this every Monday without me?
path: Sidebar → Scheduled → new task, set the timing

classes.subject: gemini

_format: Every class carries a `demo`: same task, ONE variable changed, plus the mechanism sentence explaining WHY the bad one was bad. Format spec: operations/classes/before-and-after-format.md. Understanding beats memorising.
_runtime: Ali 2026-07-22: classes run 5-10 minutes. 2 minutes is too short for most. But NEVER pad to hit a number — if a topic is honestly covered in less, it ends. IMPORTANT CORRECTION: the re-shoot argument is about SCOPE, not duration. One topic per class is what makes a rename cost one re-shoot; a 7-minute single-topic class is just as cheap to redo as a 2-minute one. Earlier reasoning conflated the two.
_slide: Every class opens on a 1999 overhead-projector transparency: class name, subject and period, and a 'Today you will' list. Built in HTML on the class page from the `learn` field — no art generation — and screen-recorded as the video's opening card.
_related: Ali 2026-07-22: every class points back into the town — a LIBRAiRY book, an episode, and an owned tool where one genuinely fits. Anyone can google a how-to; the reason to be here is that the lesson connects to something. ONLY link things that exist.
_basics: Ali 2026-07-22: EPISODES teach the thinking (what AI is, how to ask, how to check, which tool). CLASSES show the MACHINERY — the actual screens you click. Basics is therefore the elements every tool has, not concepts. Three scripts that had drifted onto episode ground were retired to operations/classes/_retired/ — see its README.
